subject: ophthalmology
title: Congenital and secondary glaucoma

steps.tx: **Primary congenital glaucoma** from trabeculodysgenesis enlarges the elastic infant eye into **buphthalmos**, with tearing, photophobia, blepharospasm and a hazy enlarged cornea crossed by Haab striae from Descemet membrane tears, all under high pressure. Clouding that clears as pressure falls differs from congenital hereditary endothelial dystrophy. Drops only bridge to theatre, and definitive treatment is surgical through **goniotomy** or trabeculotomy to open the angle, with trabeculectomy or drainage tubes for failures. Early surgery prevents amblyopia and optic nerve damage.
steps.say: A tearing and photophobic infant with a large hazy eye has congenital glaucoma until proven otherwise. The enlarged globe is buphthalmos and the corneal lines are Haab striae from pressure stretching. Drops only bridge the child to surgery, because the angle needs goniotomy or trabeculotomy. Early operation is needed before amblyopia and optic damage cause permanent vision loss.

vis.alt: Clinical image of an infant eye with buphthalmos and corneal haze. Inset shows Haab striae. Diagram illustrates trabeculodysgenesis.
vis.caption: Primary congenital glaucoma: Buphthalmos, hazy cornea with Haab striae, trabeculodysgenesis. Image: Williams AL and Bohnsack BL, CC BY 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: **Steroid induced glaucoma** blocks outflow through the trabecular meshwork in responders such as children, nearsighted patients and families with open angle glaucoma, appearing within weeks of potent drops, so each steroid course needs pressure checks. **Uveitic glaucoma** combines inflammatory debris, synechial angle closure and steroid response, and it needs inflammation control with aqueous suppressants, cautious laser and drainage tubes rather than trabeculectomy in inflamed eyes. **Pseudoexfoliation** deposits white flakes with poor dilation and weak zonules, while pigment dispersion affects young nearsighted men with Krukenberg spindles and exercise storms.
steps.say: Any prolonged steroid drop course needs scheduled pressure checks, because responders develop glaucoma within weeks. Inflammation with debris and synechiae causes uveitic glaucoma, which needs inflammation control before filtration surgery. White flakes on the lens with poor dilation indicate pseudoexfoliation with weak zonules. Pigment dispersion in a young nearsighted man can trigger pressure storms after exercise.

steps.tx: **Neovascular glaucoma**, sometimes called 100 day glaucoma after central retinal vein occlusion or with proliferative diabetic disease, grows a fibrovascular membrane across the angle and causes severe pain with very high pressure and rubeosis. Panretinal photocoagulation removes the ischaemic drive while tubes or cyclodestruction palliate pressure, since trabeculectomy fails on bleeding membranes. **Lens induced** emergencies include phacomorphic glaucoma from a swollen lens needing urgent extraction and phacolytic glaucoma from leaked protein needing washout. **Aqueous misdirection** shallows the central chamber after surgery and needs cycloplegics with vitrectomy in refractory cases.
steps.say: A red painful eye with new vessels on the iris after vein occlusion or diabetic disease is neovascular glaucoma. Laser to the ischaemic retina removes the drive, while tubes or cyclodestruction control pressure. A swollen lens that shuts the angle needs urgent extraction, and leaked lens protein needs washout. A shallow central chamber after surgery suggests aqueous misdirection, which needs cycloplegics.

steps.tx: This slit lamp photograph shows fine new vessels over the iris near the pupil with a gonioscopy inset demonstrating **angle closure**, which is the hallmark of **neovascular glaucoma**. Ischaemia from vein occlusion or diabetic disease drives a fibrovascular membrane across the drain, producing severe pain with very high pressure and visible **rubeosis**. The image matters because it directs treatment toward photocoagulation of the ischaemic retina rather than drops alone, with tubes or cyclodestruction when the angle is closed.
steps.say: This photograph shows delicate new vessels spreading over the iris toward the pupil, with angle closure in the gonioscopy inset. Retinal ischaemia from vein occlusion or diabetic disease grows this membrane across the drain. Pressure rises rapidly and becomes painful because the angle is sealed shut. Treatment must laser the ischaemic retina, while tubes or cyclodestruction palliate the pressure.

steps.tx: **Angle recession** after blunt trauma with hyphaema and a gonioscopic cleft can raise pressure months or years later, so lifetime pressure surveillance follows significant blunt injury. **Ghost cell glaucoma** from degenerate vitreous blood clogging the meshwork follows vitrectomy or trauma. Developmental angle disorders including iridocorneal endothelial syndromes, Axenfeld Rieger anomaly and aniridia with foveal hypoplasia and nystagmus need lifelong follow up. Surgical choice respects the cause, with goniotomy for congenital disease, tubes for scarred conjunctiva and cyclodestruction for blind painful eyes.
steps.say: Blunt eye injury with hyphaema needs pressure checks for life because angle recession declares itself late. Degenerate blood cells after vitrectomy or trauma can clog the meshwork as ghost cell glaucoma. Developmental disorders of the angle need lifelong follow up from childhood. Surgeons choose goniotomy for congenital eyes, tubes for scarred eyes and cyclodestruction for blind painful eyes.
